title: The Emperor's Studio: Jahangir's Court, 1615–1619
subtitle: Sir Thomas Roe's embassy, the imperial painters and the English pictures at Ajmer, Mandu and Ahmedabad, 1615–1619
intro: In September 1615 Sir Thomas Roe came ashore at Surat as James I's ambassador to the Mughal emperor Jahangir, with a treaty to win for the East India Company and a cargo of presents he already feared were too poor. He reached the court at Ajmer at the end of December and was received on 10 January 1616 (Old Style). For the next three years he followed the moving court, south to the hill-fortress of Mandu in 1617 and west to Ahmedabad in 1618, and he wrote everything down.

The court he followed was also a studio. Jahangir had grown up in his father Akbar's painting workshops and kept the finest painters in Asia: Abu'l Hasan, Mansur, the young Bichitr, and the portraitist Bishandas, who spent these same years at the Persian court taking the likeness of Shah Abbas. The English gifts, the coach, the virginals, the portraits of the royal family, a miniature in Roe's pocket and a picture of Venus with a satyr, went straight into that world of looking, copying and judging. The court's craftsmen copied the coach. The painters copied the miniature so well that Roe could not find his own by candlelight. The English king's face turned up in a Mughal allegory, waiting at the foot of Jahangir's throne.

The record is not a set of diaries in the strict sense. Roe kept a journal and a letter-book, and Coryate wrote dated letters that were printed in London within two years. Jahangir wrote a memoir in Persian, arranged by regnal year and dated by day, which was meant to be read at court as his own portrait. Terry wrote his book long afterwards. The painters left no words except signatures and inscriptions, so they are heard through their pictures and through their patron. Nur Jahan, Asaf Khan and Prince Khurram appear only in what others wrote about them, and their entries are labelled that way.

Each of these sources has a point of view, and the chapter keeps them side by side rather than choosing between them. Roe is clever and often condescending; he sees obstruction where the court saw protocol, and insult where there may only have been curiosity. Jahangir records what he wished remembered and never once names the English ambassador who sat in his hall for three years. Where the two records meet, as on the November days in 1616 when the prince rode out in a copied English coach and the emperor left Ajmer in a European carriage, they agree almost to the day while describing quite different events.

A short prologue gives William Hawkins, the first Englishman to talk with Jahangir (1609–11), and a Persian counterpoint gives Pietro della Valle, a European writing about Shah Abbas's court in the years when Bishandas was painting it.
calendar_note: English writers (Roe, Coryate, Terry, Hawkins) used the Julian calendar, ten days behind the Gregorian in these years; England did not change until 1752. Their dates are shown as written, marked O.S., and date_iso adds ten days. Jahangir dated by the solar Ilahi months inherited from Akbar (Farvardin, Urdibihisht, ... Isfandarmuz), with the Hijri lunar date often given as well. His regnal years begin at Nauroz, the sun's entry into Aries, about 20 March Gregorian, so his eleventh year began on 19 March 1616. The Rogers and Beveridge translation gives Christian equivalents in both styles: 19 March 1616 is New Style, but 10 March 1618 for the next New Year but one is Old Style. The dates here have been recomputed as Gregorian, and where Jahangir names a weekday it has been checked (24 Tir of year 13 falls on Sunday 15 July 1618). Ilahi dates converted by month-length are marked approx.

eyes.name: Nur al-Din Muhammad Jahangir
eyes.role: Fourth Mughal emperor (reigned 1605–1627), aged 46–50 in these years; patron of the imperial painting workshop
eyes.where: With the moving court: Ajmer (1613–16), the march south, Mandu (1617), Gujarat and Ahmedabad (1617–18), then north to the Punjab
eyes.vantage_label: emperor and patron, writing his own record
eyes.authenticity: The Jahangirnama (also called Tuzuk-i Jahangiri) was written or dictated by Jahangir himself and arranged by regnal years, with entries dated by day in the solar Ilahi months and often by the Hijri date as well. He wrote it up to his seventeenth regnal year, and Mu'tamad Khan continued it. It is a deliberate self-portrait, made for circulation at court. It never names Sir Thomas Roe. The English translation by Alexander Rogers, edited by Henry Beveridge (2 vols, 1909–14), is used here; the modern translation by W. M. Thackston (1999) is not quoted.
eyes.bio: Jahangir had grown up in his father Akbar's workshops and claimed an expert's eye. His memoir records animals, plants, weighings, hunts, gifts and painters as closely as it records campaigns. It is the only record here written by the man everyone else was trying to please, and also a record of how he wished to be seen.

sources.title: The Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, trans. Rogers, ed. Beveridge, vol. 1 (1909), Project Gutenberg

eyes.name: Sir Thomas Roe
eyes.role: English ambassador from James I to Jahangir, paid by the East India Company; aged about 34 on arrival
eyes.side: English crown and East India Company
eyes.where: Surat, then Ajmer (1616), Mandu (1617) and Ahmedabad (1618) with the court
eyes.vantage_label: foreign ambassador in the audience hall
eyes.authenticity: Roe's journal and letter-book survive in a copy made by his secretary Edward Heynes (British Library Add. MS 6115). Samuel Purchas printed an abridged journal in 1625, and Robert Kerr reprinted that abridgment in modernised spelling in the 1810s. William Foster edited the full text for the Hakluyt Society (1899; revised 1926). Dates are Julian (Old Style). Quotations here are from Purchas or Foster as cited.
eyes.bio: Roe came to win a treaty and found a court where favour moved through gifts, pictures and private evenings. His journal is sharp, impatient and often condescending, but it is the closest record of the painting workshop at work: the copied miniature, the portraits on the wall behind the throne and the arguments over what a picture meant.

eyes.name: Thomas Coryate (Coryat)
eyes.role: English traveller and writer, who walked overland from Jerusalem to India; aged about 38 at Ajmer
eyes.side: English, travelling on his own account
eyes.where: Ajmer (July 1615–Sept 1616), then Agra; died at Surat, December 1617
eyes.authenticity: His letters from India were printed in London in two pamphlets, Thomas Coriate Traveller for the English Wits: Greeting (1616) and Mr Thomas Coriat to his Friends in England Sendeth Greeting (1618). Purchas reprinted a selection. William Foster reprinted them from the pamphlets in Early Travels in India (1921).
eyes.bio: Coryate had no office, little money and great nerve. He learned Persian, made a speech to the emperor from below the palace window and wrote home to the Mermaid Tavern wits. His letters show the court from the street, where money was thrown from a window.

sources.title: Foster (ed.), Early Travels in India 1583–1619 (1921), Internet Archive text

eyes.name: Rev. Edward Terry
eyes.role: Chaplain with the 1616 East India Company fleet, then chaplain to Roe from early 1617; aged about 26
eyes.where: Surat (Sept 1616), then with Roe at Mandu and on the march to Gujarat
eyes.authenticity: Terry's short account was printed by Purchas in 1625. He expanded it greatly as A Voyage to East-India (1655), nearly forty years after the events, with sermons and later reflection added. The 1655 text is later and is flagged as such wherever it is used.
eyes.bio: Terry joined the embassy just as the presents from the 1616 fleet reached court. He was standing beside Roe when Jahangir asked him what an English picture meant. His later book is warmer about Mughal India than Roe's journal and gives the fullest English portrait of Coryate.

sources.title: Kerr, General History and Collection of Voyages, vol. 9 (Roe's journal and Terry from Purchas), Project Gutenberg

eyes.name: William Hawkins
eyes.role: Commander of the East India Company's Hector and the first English envoy at Jahangir's court (1609–11)
eyes.form: narrative report (written after his return to the coast)
eyes.authenticity: His relation to the Company was printed by Purchas in 1625 and reprinted by Foster in Early Travels in India (1921). It is a retrospective report, not a day-book.
eyes.bio: Hawkins spoke Turkish with the emperor, was given a rank of 400 horse and an Armenian bride, and lost favour within two years. His account is the prologue to Roe's: an Englishman finding that the court rewarded talk and curiosities more than trade.

sources.title: Foster (ed.), Early Travels in India 1583–1619 (1921), Internet Archive text

eyes.name: Mirza Abu'l Hasan, Asaf Khan
eyes.role: Senior noble, brother of Nur Jahan and father-in-law of Prince Khurram; the courtier through whom Roe's business passed
eyes.where: Ajmer, Mandu and Ahmedabad with the court
eyes.vantage_label: broker between the ambassador and the throne
eyes.form: through others' records (Roe's journal; Jahangir's memoir)
eyes.authenticity: No diary or letters of his own are used here. Everything comes from Roe's journal, which treats him with suspicion, and from Jahangir's memoir. His personal name was Abu'l Hasan, so he is not to be confused with the painter Abu'l Hasan.
eyes.bio: Asaf Khan stood in the door between Roe and the emperor. He carried messages, stopped the ambassador's interpreter, made and withdrew a bet on the painter and hung the emperor's portrait round Roe's neck. Roe saw him as an obstacle; in the court's own terms he was guarding his family's position.

sources.title: Roe's journal, September 1615–May 1616 (Kerr's reprint)
Roe's journal, June–August 1616 (Kerr's reprint)

eyes.name: Mihr al-Nisa, Nur Jahan Begam
eyes.role: Jahangir's wife from 1611, styled Nur Mahal and from March 1616 Nur Jahan; aged about 39
eyes.where: Within the household at Ajmer, Mandu and Ahmedabad
eyes.form: through others' records (Jahangir's memoir; Roe's journal)
eyes.authenticity: No diary of hers survives. Farmans and seals in her name exist, but the entries here use only what Jahangir and Roe wrote down. Roe's remarks on her influence are court report, not observation. Later legends about her are left out.
eyes.bio: Nur Jahan's power was felt by everyone in this chapter, though she never speaks in it directly. Jahangir records her titles and her marksmanship. Roe records her coach in the procession and the rumour that a prince's journey was cancelled at her urging.

sources.title: The Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, trans. Rogers, ed. Beveridge, vol. 1 (1909), Project Gutenberg

Roe's journal, October–November 1616 (Kerr's reprint)

eyes.name: Prince Khurram (later Shah Jahan)
eyes.role: Third son of Jahangir, aged 23–26; governor of Surat and from 1616 commander for the Deccan; titled Shah Jahan in October 1617
eyes.vantage_label: prince controlling the port the English needed
eyes.form: through others' records (Roe's journal; Jahangir's memoir)
eyes.authenticity: His own later court histories (the Padshahnama) belong to his reign as emperor and are not used here. Entries rest on Roe's journal and his father's memoir.
eyes.bio: Khurram held Surat, so the English treaty ran through him, and Roe found him cold, proud and slow. He later became the great builder-emperor Shah Jahan. In these years his father gave him an English-style coach and a new title.

eyes.name: Abu'l Hasan, Nadir al-Zaman
eyes.role: Court painter, son of the Herat painter Aqa Riza; aged about 27–30 in these years
eyes.form: signed and inscribed paintings (with his patron's memoir)
eyes.authenticity: He left no writings. His record is his signed or inscribed pictures, whose dates are museum estimates unless dated on the page, and what Jahangir wrote about him. Ascriptions on Mughal album pages were sometimes added later.
eyes.bio: Jahangir says he raised Abu'l Hasan from childhood and watched his art grow. In 1618 he gave him the title Nadir al-Zaman, 'Wonder of the Age', for the accession picture painted as the frontispiece of the memoir. His allegories of Jahangir were painted in the same years in which Roe watched the court.

sources.title: The Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, trans. Rogers, ed. Beveridge, vol. 2 (1914), Project Gutenberg
Freer Gallery of Art F1945.9a: Emperor Jahangir Embraces Shah Abbas

eyes.name: Ustad Mansur, Nadir al-'Asr
eyes.role: Court painter, the master of birds, animals and plants
eyes.authenticity: His record is his signed natural-history studies and Jahangir's notices of what he was ordered to paint. Many birds and plants are attributed to him on style alone; only signed or documented works are used here.
eyes.bio: When a strange bird reached court, or a gift died, Jahangir sent for Mansur. His turkey cock, signed as the work of the slave of the court, records an American bird that came through Portuguese Goa. His title Nadir al-'Asr, 'Wonder of the Time', was confirmed in the memoir in 1618.

sources.title: V&A IM.135-1921: a turkey cock, by Mansur
The Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, trans. Rogers, ed. Beveridge, vol. 2 (1914), Project Gutenberg

eyes.name: Bichitr
eyes.role: Young court painter, just beginning his career in these years
eyes.vantage_label: painter who put the English king into a Mughal allegory
eyes.authenticity: Known only from his signed works. The Freer Gallery dates the picture used here to about 1615–1618; it is not dated on the page.
eyes.bio: Bichitr painted Jahangir on an hourglass throne handing a book to a Sufi shaikh while an Ottoman sultan and James I of England wait below. He painted himself in the corner holding a small picture. The English king's face was taken from an English portrait of the kind Roe's embassy brought.

sources.title: Freer Gallery of Art F1942.15a: Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings
Smarthistory: Bichitr, Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings

eyes.name: Bishandas
eyes.role: Court portrait painter, sent with the embassy of Khan Alam to Shah Abbas of Persia
eyes.authenticity: His mission is recorded in Jahangir's memoir. Portraits of Shah Abbas attributed to him survive in several collections, but none is used here as dated evidence.
eyes.bio: While Roe studied the Mughal court, Bishandas was studying the Persian one. Jahangir says he was unequalled at taking likenesses and sent him to bring back the faces of Shah Abbas and his nobles. Those faces then fed the court's allegories of the two rulers.

sources.title: The Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, trans. Rogers, ed. Beveridge, vol. 2 (1914), Project Gutenberg

eyes.name: Pietro della Valle
eyes.role: Roman nobleman and traveller in Safavid Persia, aged about 31
eyes.where: Isfahan (1617), the shah's camp in Mazandaran and the north-west (1618)
eyes.vantage_label: European eyewitness at the rival court
eyes.authenticity: His 36 long letters were addressed to Mario Schipano in Naples and published as the Viaggi (vol. 1 in 1650; the rest in 1658). He reworked some of them before publication.
eyes.bio: Della Valle gives a European view of Shah Abbas's court in the years when Bishandas was painting there. He is a counterweight to Roe: another proud European trying to read an Islamic court, but this time the court whose ruler Jahangir most wanted to equal.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Della Valle, Pietro

entries.headline: Hawkins reaches Agra and talks Turkish with the emperor
entries.digest: Hawkins reached Agra after a long journey up from Surat with the Company's letter. Jahangir found that he could talk to him in Turkish without an interpreter and kept him for long conversations about the West. He gave him a rank of 400 horse and the style of khan. Hawkins read the favour as a trading opening, but it lasted less than two years.
entries.source_note: Hawkins's relation, in Foster, Early Travels in India (1921), from Purchas 1625.

entries.headline: Mansur paints the turkey that came by way of Goa
entries.digest: Mansur painted a turkey cock in profile, set against a plain ground with streaks of cloud with a strip of flowers at the base. The bird was an American species that had reached court through Jahangir's agent at Portuguese Goa. Under the wattle Mansur signed it as the work of the slave of the court, the Wonder of the Age. The V&A links the picture to the bird's arrival in 1612, which Jahangir noted in his memoir.
entries.source_note: V&A IM.135-1921 catalogue entry (date c. 1612; signature as translated by the museum).

entries.place: Agra, about to leave for Ajmer
entries.headline: Khan Alam is sent to Persia, a painter in his train
entries.digest: Jahangir recalled Khan Alam from the Deccan and gave him leave to go to Shah Abbas as ambassador, travelling with the returning Persian envoy. Years later the memoir explains that the painter Bishandas went with him to bring back likenesses of the shah and his chief men. The mission kept a Mughal painter at the Safavid court for the whole of Roe's embassy.
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 1, p. 248 (leave to Khan Alam); vol. 2, pp. 116–17 (Bishandas sent with him).

entries.headline: News of an English sea-fight off Surat
entries.digest: Jahangir noted that a fight had taken place at Surat between the English and the Portuguese. This was the Company's defence of its ships at Swally in early 1615. The memoir treats it as one item of frontier news among many, but the English win off Surat helped Roe's embassy follow that year.
entries.quote: a fight took place between the English
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 1, p. 274.

entries.headline: Roe lands at Surat and finds his chests searched
entries.digest: Roe came ashore at Surat after more than six months at sea and was received by the port officials. He was angered when his servants and baggage were searched, and saw it as an insult to his king. He spent a month arguing before he set out inland on 30 October.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal, Kerr's reprint of Purchas (sect. 6a); Foster's edition (1899).

entries.headline: Coryate writes home from 'the court of the Great Mogul'
entries.digest: Coryate dated two letters from Ajmer on Michaelmas day, one to his friend Laurence Whitaker and one to Sir Edward Phelips. The letters, with a postscript of 8 November, reported that an English ambassador had landed at Surat. He described the emperor showing himself three times a day at a palace window hung with embroidery and set on silver pillars. He also noted his own plan to ride an elephant and print a picture of it.
entries.quote: that hath an embroidered sumptuous coverture
entries.source_note: Coryate, Letters I–II (printed 1616), in Foster, Early Travels in India (1921).

entries.headline: Roe reaches Ajmer, sick, with Coryate as company
entries.digest: Roe reached Ajmer too ill to leave his bed for some days. On the road just before, William Edwards of the Company and Thomas Coryate had come out to meet him (Kerr's text places the meeting at Chitor on 18 December). Roe later wrote that Coryate had arrived as if sent by fate to keep him company.
entries.quote: whom the fates have sent hither to ease mee
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, sect. 6a); Roe's letter quoted in Foster, Early Travels in India (1921), Coryat introduction.

entries.headline: First audience: the king's letter and the English coach
entries.digest: At about four in the afternoon Roe went to the durbar and presented James I's letter, his commission and the Company's presents. Jahangir received them kindly, asked questions and offered him his own physicians. The chief gift was an English coach. Roe went home believing he had been received with unusual favour.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, sect. 6a, with editor's note on the coach); Foster's edition.

entries.headline: Roe meets the prince who holds Surat
entries.digest: Roe called on Prince Khurram, who received him in a private room. The prince governed Surat, where the English had their factory, so every grievance over customs and searches ran through his officers. Roe noted the visit as a courtesy. In fact it began the long struggle at the centre of his embassy.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, sect. 6a).

entries.headline: Roe reports the coach and the virginals to the Company
entries.digest: Writing to the Company, Roe listed what he had given: the coach, a set of virginals, knives, an embroidered scarf and a sword. Jahangir had the English musician play the virginals and rode in the coach. Roe named Asaf Khan as the man to win and Nur Mahal as the king's beloved wife. He also warned that English presents looked poor beside what others brought.
entries.source_note: Calendar of State Papers, East Indies, no. 1086 (British History Online).

entries.headline: English portraits behind the throne at Nauroz
entries.digest: For the New Year festival a throne was set up in the durbar court, and English pictures hung behind it. Roe listed portraits of James I, Queen Anne, Princess Elizabeth, two countesses, a London citizen's wife and Sir Thomas Smythe, the Company's governor. Prince Khurram's pavilion stood to one side. The nobles came up to present their gifts. Roe saw his king's face used to decorate another king's festival.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, sect. 6a); RCT, Eastern Encounters, ch. 1 (portraits shown at Nauroz in 1616 and 1617). Roe's opening date falls about a week before the equinox by Jahangir's reckoning, so the day is approximate.

entries.date_display: 1 Farvardin, regnal year 11; 1 Rabi I 1025 (19 March 1616)
entries.place: Ajmer, the hall of public audience
entries.headline: Jahangir's eleventh New Year, among European screens
entries.digest: Jahangir recorded the sun's entry into Aries and the start of his eleventh regnal year. The hall of audience was decorated, he noted, with European screens and hangings, and the nobles brought their offerings day by day. He does not mention the English ambassador who sat watching.
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 1, pp. 318–19.

entries.headline: Asaf Khan blocks Roe's interpreter
entries.digest: At the evening private audience Asaf Khan tried to keep out Roe's Italian interpreter, for fear of what the ambassador might say to the emperor without a filter. Roe forced his way to raising the treaty. Jahangir thought Roe was accusing the prince, and the quarrel had to be smoothed over. Roe saw only obstruction. Asaf Khan was guarding the access on which his family's power rested.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, sect. 6a).

entries.date_display: the eleventh day of the New Year feast, regnal year 11 (late March 1616)
entries.headline: Nur Mahal becomes Nur Jahan
entries.digest: On the eleventh day of the New Year feast Jahangir ordered that his wife, until then styled Nur Mahal, 'Light of the Palace', should be called Nur Jahan Begam, 'Light of the World'. The memoir makes it a single line among the festival honours. Roe's journal continued to call her Normahal.
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 1, p. 319. The Gregorian day is counted from 19 March.

entries.headline: The emperor feasts at Asaf Khan's house
entries.digest: Jahangir dined at Asaf Khan's house. Roe recorded the report that the feast and its presents cost six lakhs of rupees. Whatever the true sum, he understood that a nobleman's standing was shown by what he could lay before the throne.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, sect. 6a, with editor's conversion of the sum).

entries.headline: A miniature is shown and a painter makes a boast
entries.digest: Jahangir had heard that Roe kept an excellent painter. Roe explained that this was a young merchant, Mr Hughes, who only drew with a pen for pleasure. That night Roe showed the emperor a small portrait of a friend that he carried, and Jahangir passed it round his court. The chief painter said he could copy it so well that no one would know the difference. Roe doubted it, and Asaf Khan laid a horse on the outcome, though he later withdrew the bet.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, sect. 6b); RCT, Eastern Encounters, ch. 1, citing Purchas 1625, I, pp. 546–8.

entries.headline: Six pictures by candlelight: which is the English one?
entries.digest: Jahangir sent for Roe late at night and showed him six small portraits pasted on one board, his own miniature and five copies by the chief painter. By candlelight Roe could not at first tell them apart, and the emperor was delighted. With a closer look Roe found his own and pointed out the differences. He offered the painter fifty rupees, but Jahangir said the man was a gentleman. Roe was told to choose one copy to take home and asked instead for a portrait of the emperor himself.
entries.quote: troubled to discerne which was which
entries.source_note: Roe's journal, Purchas 1625, I, pp. 546–8, as quoted in RCT, Eastern Encounters, ch. 1; Kerr's reprint (sect. 6b).

entries.headline: Asaf Khan hangs the emperor's portrait on Roe
entries.digest: Jahangir sent Roe a small portrait of himself set in gold, on a gold chain with a pendant pearl, through Asaf Khan. Roe had been warned that the custom was to touch the ground with the head on receiving it. Asaf Khan had him take off his hat and put the picture round his neck, and Roe thanked the emperor in the English manner. Some officers called for the prostration, but Jahangir let it go. Roe valued the jewel at under thirty pounds and noted it was five times grander than the usual medal.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, sect. 6b).

entries.headline: The solar weighing 'in the usual manner'
entries.digest: Jahangir noted that his solar birthday weighing was held as usual, For him it was a fixed rite of the year, recorded in a line.
entries.quote: the meeting for my solar weighing was held
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 1, pp. 332–3. The Ilahi date and Roe's Julian date do not convert to the same day, so the month only is given.

entries.place: Ajmer, the palace garden and the ghusalkhana
entries.headline: Roe misses the weighing, then shows his pictures at ten at night
entries.digest: Roe arrived too late, after a messenger's mistake, to see the emperor weighed against gold, silver, silk, grain and fruit. At about ten that night Jahangir sent for him and asked to see a picture Roe owned. Roe brought two. The emperor wanted one, then agreed to have copies made for his wives and return the original. Roe was given strong wine in a gold cup and the cup itself, set with rubies and turquoises.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, sect. 6c).

entries.headline: Roe hears that Nur Mahal has stopped a prince's visit
entries.digest: Roe recorded the court report that Prince Parvez, camped a few miles off and anxious to see his father, had first been allowed to come and then ordered away to Bengal at Nur Mahal's urging. This was Roe's reading of court gossip, but it shows how far her influence was assumed. Khurram, her ally, stood to gain.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, sect. 6c). Hearsay in the original, reported as such.

entries.headline: Terry's fleet anchors after a fight with a Portuguese carrack
entries.digest: The six-ship fleet in which Terry sailed as chaplain anchored at Swally Road. Off the Comoros it had fought a Portuguese carrack, and its commander, Benjamin Joseph, had been killed. Thomas Kerridge and the Surat merchants came aboard. The fleet carried the next batch of presents for the emperor, the ones Jahangir would open himself at Mandu.
entries.source_note: Terry's account (Purchas 1625), Kerr's reprint, vol. 9, sect. 7.

entries.headline: The Persian ambassador's gifts outshine the English
entries.digest: The Persian ambassador presented his first gifts at the durbar, and within days Jahangir rewarded him with 20,000 rupees. Roe compared them with his own presents and felt the comparison painfully. According to a Jesuit, the emperor later remarked that the English king sent gifts of very small value. Among the gifts at court in these weeks Roe noted velvet woven with Italian pictures and Venetian tapestry.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, sect. 6e); RCT, Eastern Encounters, ch. 1.

entries.headline: Coryate's Persian speech and the silver thrown from the window
entries.digest: Writing to his mother from Agra, Coryate set out the speech he had made in Persian to the emperor below the palace window, addressing him as Lord Protector of the World. He asked for a pass to Samarkand. Jahangir answered that the Tartars would probably kill a Christian, and had a hundred silver pieces let down to him in a sheet. Roe had disapproved of the begging. Coryate also described the emperor weighing himself on his birthday.
entries.quote: weighed himselfe in a paire of golden scales
entries.source_note: Coryate, Letter V (printed 1618), in Foster, Early Travels in India (1921). The date of the oration itself is not given in the letter.

entries.headline: An English-style carriage for the prince
entries.digest: As Khurram left Ajmer to command in the Deccan, Jahangir gave him a robe, horses, an elephant and weapons, and a carriage made in the English fashion. The memoir presents it as a mark of imperial favour. The translators' footnote adds Roe's correction: it was not the English coach but a copy made at court.
entries.quote: a carriage, according to the English fashion
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 1, pp. 338–9 and note 41.

entries.headline: Roe watches the prince ride out in a copied coach
entries.digest: Roe recorded the prince leaving court loaded with presents, among them a coach made to resemble the English one. To Roe it showed that the court's craftsmen could reproduce English goods as easily as its painters copied English pictures. To the court it was simply one more fine carriage for the prince.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, sect. 6e); compare Tuzuk vol. 1, p. 339 note 41.

entries.date_display: Saturday 1 Dhu'l-Qa'da 1025 = 21 Aban, regnal year 11 (12 November 1616)
entries.headline: The emperor leaves Ajmer in the Frank carriage
entries.digest: Jahangir left Ajmer for the south at the hour chosen by his astrologers. He rode out in a European carriage drawn by four horses. The memoir names the vehicle but not who had given it. His nobles followed on elephants and horses.
entries.quote: mounted the Frank carriage, which had four horses attached
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 1, p. 340 (the text says Tuesday; the translators' note corrects the weekday to Saturday).

entries.headline: Women behind the screen, and Nur Mahal's coach
entries.digest: Roe watched the emperor go out to his tents. At a latticed window above, the royal women made holes in the screen to look at the Englishman, and he could see their eyes and hands. In the procession he noted Nur Mahal's coach and the blinded Prince Khusrau. Two weeks later the camp at Ajmer was burned and the town emptied, and Roe had to buy carts because no camels came.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, sect. 6e).

entries.headline: Bichitr puts James I below a Sufi shaikh
entries.digest: Bichitr painted Jahangir on an hourglass throne, inside a great halo, handing a book to an old Sufi shaikh. Below wait an Ottoman sultan and James I of England, and in the corner Bichitr himself holds a small painting. The English king's face follows a portrait by John de Critz, believed to have come to court with Roe's embassy. Putti borrowed from European art float above. The inscriptions say the emperor prefers holy men to kings.
entries.source_note: Freer Gallery F1942.15a (date c. 1615–1618); Smarthistory essay (source portrait by de Critz, believed given by Roe).

entries.headline: A tamarind tree for the illustrations
entries.digest: Camped by a lake near Ujjain, Jahangir described a remarkable tamarind tree and told his artists to put it into the illustrations of the Jahangirnama. The order shows the memoir and its pictures being made together, on the road, as the court moved.
entries.quote: I told my artists to depict it
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 1, p. 353. The Ilahi month of the entry is not clear in the copy consulted.

entries.headline: Jahangir writes to James I asking for rarities
entries.digest: Jahangir answered James I's letter with a letter of his own, written in the months when Roe was pressing for a farman. In it he asked for rarities and rich goods suitable for his palaces. The request shows what he wanted from England: curiosities and fine things, more than trade.
entries.source_note: British Library Add. MS 4155, fol. 100, cited in RCT, Eastern Encounters, ch. 1.

entries.headline: Della Valle reaches Isfahan and waits for the shah
entries.digest: Della Valle crossed the snowbound passes of Kurdistan from Baghdad and reached Isfahan. Shah Abbas was away in the north, so he waited almost a year in the capital, learning Persian and studying the court. Somewhere in that court the Mughal embassy, with its painter, was doing the same.
entries.source_note: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Della Valle, Pietro'.

entries.headline: Terry sees the New Year festival at 'Mandoa'
entries.digest: Terry, newly attached to the embassy, saw the New Year celebrations at Mandu, where the emperor had a great palace. He described the festival and the gifts poured out before the throne. He wrote it up years later as a set piece of Mughal splendour.
entries.source_note: Terry's account in Purchas 1625 (Kerr's reprint, vol. 9, sect. 7); expanded in his Voyage to East-India (1655).

entries.headline: The court enters Mandu
entries.digest: Jahangir entered the buildings prepared for him in the old fortress-city of Mandu, on its plateau above the Narmada. His builder Abdul Karim had been sent ahead months before to repair the palaces. He planned to oversee the Deccan war from there.
entries.quote: I entered the houses which they had prepared
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 1, p. 363 (and p. 281 for the builder sent ahead).

entries.headline: Roe camps in a ruined courtyard with a tomb
entries.digest: Roe reached Mandu with the camp and found almost no shelter. He took over a walled courtyard that held an old temple and a tomb, and set up his household there. Over the following months a lion and a wolf would get into the yard at night.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, vol. 9, sect. 6, Mandu portion).

entries.headline: A New Year gift of knives and glasses
entries.digest: At the New Year festival Roe presented knives and glassware, and Jahangir seated him beside the Persian ambassador. Above the throne hung the portraits of James I. The English pictures had come with the court from Ajmer and were displayed again.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, vol. 9, Mandu portion); RCT, Eastern Encounters, ch. 1.

entries.date_display: between 12 March and 25 May 1617 (O.S.); undated in Purchas's abridgment
entries.headline: Venus leading a satyr: the emperor asks what it means
entries.digest: Jahangir had the chests of new presents brought to him and opened them himself, taking mastiffs, embroidered bags, glass cases, hats his women liked and the pictures. One picture showed Venus leading a satyr by the nose. He had his nobles explain it, pointing to the satyr's horns and dark skin, and Roe suspected the court read it as a mockery of Asians ruled by a woman. Roe said it was only the painter's invention. When the emperor asked Terry's opinion, Roe answered for him. He kept his anger behind polite words.
entries.quote: a picture of Venus leading a satyr by the nose
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, vol. 9, Mandu portion, from Purchas 1625).

entries.headline: Nur Jahan shoots four tigers
entries.digest: The huntsmen had marked down four tigers, and Nur Jahan shot them from a howdah on an elephant, killing two with a single shot each. Jahangir gave her bracelets worth a lakh (100,000) of rupees. The memoir presents her skill with open pride.
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 1, p. 375. Gregorian day counted from the New Year of 20 March 1617.

entries.headline: The second weighing, and thin silver nuts
entries.digest: This time Roe was present. Jahangir sat in the scales against bags of silver, then gold, jewels, cloth, spices and grain, and the silver was set aside for the poor. He then threw basins of silver almonds and spices to his nobles. Roe caught a handful and found the 'nuts' so thin that the whole was worth about twenty rupees. He left before the drinking because he was unwell.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, vol. 9, Mandu portion).

entries.headline: A Mercator atlas for the emperor
entries.digest: As Jahangir rode past his house, Roe gave him a Mercator atlas. The emperor put his hand on his breast and said that anything from Roe was welcome. Later the book was sent back because none of his learned men could read it. Roe took that as a sign of the court's limits, though the court may simply have found no use for a Latin atlas.
entries.source_note: Roe's journal (Kerr, vol. 9, Mandu portion).

entries.headline: Khurram returns victorious and becomes Shah Jahan
entries.digest: Back from the Deccan with a settlement and great presents, Khurram was received at Mandu, and his father gave him the title Shah Jahan, 'King of the World'. He had earlier been styled Shah during the campaign.
entries.quote: bestowed on him the title of Shah Jahan
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 1, Mandu section, entry for 20 Mihr of regnal year 12.

entries.headline: Coryate dies at Surat
entries.digest: Coryate died at Surat in December 1617, aged about forty, still far from home. Terry later wrote the fullest English portrait of him in his Voyage to East-India, nearly forty years afterwards. Coryate never reached Samarkand.
entries.source_note: Foster, Early Travels in India (1921), Coryat introduction (death at Surat, December 1617); Terry, A Voyage to East-India (1655), written later.

entries.headline: Abu'l Hasan paints Jahangir embracing Shah Abbas
entries.digest: Abu'l Hasan painted Jahangir, large and haloed, embracing a smaller Shah Abbas as the two stand on a lion and a lamb over a globe. The Freer calls it wish-fulfilment: the two rulers never met, and they were rivals over Qandahar. The shah's features in such pictures are generally linked to the portraits Bishandas was making in Persia.
entries.source_note: Freer Gallery F1945.9a (date c. 1618, artist Abu'l Hasan, label text). The link to Bishandas is a scholarly position, not stated on the label.

entries.headline: Della Valle goes north to find Shah Abbas
entries.digest: Della Valle set out from Isfahan through Kashan, Firuzkuh and the Alborz to the shah's court at Farahabad on the Caspian side. He then followed Shah Abbas and the army toward Ardabil against the Ottoman threat. His letters describe a ruler always on the move, much as Roe described Jahangir.
entries.source_note: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Della Valle, Pietro'.

entries.headline: The emperor calls Ahmedabad 'Dust-town'
entries.digest: Jahangir entered Ahmedabad again. Disliking its dust, its water and the sickness there, he wrote that he had already renamed it Gardabad, 'abode of dust'. He sat at the palace window to hear complaints all the same. Roe was in the city with the court in these months.
entries.quote: I had already called Aḥmadābād Gardābād
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 2, pp. 9 and 13–14.

entries.headline: Titles for two painters, and a boast of the expert eye
entries.digest: Jahangir rewarded Abu'l Hasan for the picture of his accession painted as the frontispiece of the Jahangirnama and gave him the title Nadir al-Zaman. He wrote that Ustad Mansur, Nadir al-'Asr, was his equal in drawing, and that in his father's reign and his own these two had no third. Then he boasted that he could tell, without being told, which painter had made each face in a group picture, even who had painted the eyes and eyebrows.
entries.quote: drew the picture of my accession as the frontispiece
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 2, pp. 20–21. Weekday checked: 15 July 1618 (Gregorian) was a Sunday.

entries.headline: Victory celebrations at Qazvin
entries.digest: After a season's campaign in which Tabriz was briefly lost and then saved, Shah Abbas held victory celebrations at Qazvin. Della Valle was there, then fell ill and went back to Isfahan, while the shah went to his winter quarters by the Caspian. It was the Persian court at its most confident, the court Jahangir's painters were trying to outdo.
entries.source_note: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Della Valle, Pietro'.

entries.headline: Roe sails for England
entries.digest: Roe had left the court in Gujarat the previous year with letters and a set of farmans, but no formal treaty. He sailed from Surat for England early in 1619. In his reports he advised the Company to keep to trade and avoid forts and wars.
entries.source_note: Standard chronology of the embassy (Foster's edition, 1899); departure details not checked against the journal for this chapter.

entries.place: Imperial camp, on the way north
entries.headline: A dead falcon is sent to Mansur
entries.digest: Shah Abbas had sent Jahangir a royal falcon by an envoy, Pari Beg. One bird died on the road, and the falcon that reached court died soon after. Jahangir ordered Ustad Mansur to paint its likeness before it was lost. The order shows how his painters worked as the court's recorders of natural things.
entries.quote: I ordered Ustād Manṣūr, who has the title
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 2, p. 108. Weekday checked: 10 November 1619 (Gregorian) was a Sunday.

entries.headline: Bishandas comes home with the shah's face
entries.digest: Khan Alam returned from Persia and paid his respects at the Kalanaur garden. With him came Bishandas, whom Jahangir had sent to take the likenesses of the shah and his chief men. Jahangir wrote that he had painted most of them well, and the shah's portrait above all, and he rewarded the painter with an elephant. After six years the painter's faces were now in the emperor's hands.
entries.quote: especially had taken that of my brother the Shah
entries.source_note: Tuzuk, trans. Rogers & Beveridge, vol. 2, pp. 115–17. Weekday checked: 23 January 1620 (Gregorian) was a Thursday.

convergences.label: Nauroz at Ajmer, March 1616
convergences.note: In the same festival weeks Roe saw English portraits hung behind the throne, Jahangir recorded European screens in his hall, Nur Mahal became Nur Jahan, and Asaf Khan tried to keep Roe's interpreter out. The memoir records the decoration; the ambassador records being used as it.

convergences.label: The copying contest
convergences.note: Roe's journal is the only record of the night of six pictures. Jahangir's memoir never mentions it, but two years later he wrote that he could tell any painter's hand at sight, a boast the contest put to the test from the other side. Asaf Khan made the wager and later hung the emperor's portrait round Roe's neck.

convergences.label: The birthday weighing at Ajmer
convergences.note: Jahangir notes the weighing in a line. Roe misses it through a messenger's error but is summoned at ten that night to show his pictures. Coryate describes the golden scales to his mother. Three writers, three distances from the scales.

convergences.label: Leaving Ajmer: the coach and its copy
convergences.note: The memoir and the journal agree almost to the day. Khurram rides out on 11 November (Jahangir's 20 Aban, Roe's 1 November) in a coach Jahangir calls English-fashion and Roe calls a copy. The next day the emperor leaves in the Frank carriage, while Roe watches the women's eyes behind the screen and Nur Jahan's coach in the line.

convergences.label: Into Mandu, and the Nauroz of 1617
convergences.note: Jahangir enters his repaired palaces on the day Roe's Old Style journal calls 3 March. Roe camps in a ruined courtyard with a tomb. A week later both record the New Year, and Terry, newly arrived, writes it up as a spectacle.

convergences.label: The chests opened at Mandu
convergences.note: Jahangir opened the presents himself and asked what an English Venus and satyr meant. Roe suspected an insult was being read into it, and Terry was asked for his opinion and silenced by Roe. A few weeks earlier Jahangir had written to James I asking for rarities, so the seized chests were what he had asked for.

convergences.label: Titles in the workshop
convergences.note: At Ahmedabad Jahangir ranked his painters in writing: Abu'l Hasan and Mansur were the wonders of the age. In the same years the younger Bichitr was painting the English king into a Mughal allegory. The painters speak only through their signatures, and the emperor speaks for them.

convergences.label: Two courts, one rivalry
convergences.note: Della Valle watched Shah Abbas at Farahabad and Qazvin while Bishandas was taking the shah's likeness for Jahangir. In Abu'l Hasan's allegory the shah is smaller and in Jahangir's arms. In the European letters he is the most formidable ruler in Asia.

ties.note: They met on the road to Ajmer at the end of 1615 and shared lodgings. Roe welcomed his company but disapproved of his begging speech to the emperor.
Terry joined Roe as chaplain in 1617 and stood beside him at the opening of the chests, where Roe answered for him.
Asaf Khan was Roe's go-between and, in Roe's eyes, his chief obstacle: he carried messages, controlled access and placed the bet on the painter.
The prince governed Surat. Roe spent three years negotiating farmans with his officers and found him proud and slow.
Married in 1611. He renamed her Nur Jahan in March 1616 and recorded her hunting with pride.
Brother and sister, children of Itimad al-Daula. Their family's hold on the court is the background of Roe's frustrations.
Khurram had married Asaf Khan's daughter Arjumand Banu (later Mumtaz Mahal) in 1612, which tied the prince to Nur Jahan's family.
Father and son. The English-style coach and the title Shah Jahan were both gifts from father to son in these years.
Jahangir says he raised Abu'l Hasan from childhood, rewarded him for the accession frontispiece and named him Nadir al-Zaman.
The emperor sent Mansur the creatures he wanted recorded, from the turkey of 1612 to the falcon of 1619.
Bichitr's James I follows an English portrait by John de Critz. Smarthistory reports that it is believed to have been given by Roe, but this is not proved.
The likenesses of Shah Abbas that Bishandas made in Persia are generally linked to the shah's face in Abu'l Hasan's allegories. This is a scholarly position.
Both were at Shah Abbas's court in 1617–18, one painting it and one writing it. Neither is known to have recorded the other.
Coryate made his Persian speech beneath the palace window. Jahangir answered with advice and a hundred silver pieces let down in a sheet.

threads_out.note: Jahangir was the prince Salim of Akbar's Fatehpur Sikri, and the workshop he inherited was Akbar's. He wrote that Abu'l Hasan and Mansur had no equals in his father's reign or his own. Abu'l Hasan's father, Aqa Riza of Herat, had joined Salim's service while Akbar still ruled.

Two centuries after Clavijo's Castilian embassy to Timur, an English ambassador sat at the court of Timur's descendant. Coryate's Persian speech asked Jahangir for a pass to Samarkand, Timur's city, and the Mughal allegories of these years show angels holding Jahangir's descent from Timur.

The Royal Collection's account of the English gifts to Jahangir lists telescopes among them, less than a decade after Galileo turned the new instrument on the sky. They went to India as curiosities for a collector-emperor, not as tools of astronomy.
The Company that paid for Roe's embassy to ask a Mughal emperor for trading rights ended, in 1857–58, by deposing the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah II, a descendant of Jahangir and Shah Jahan.

images.title: Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings
images.caption: Bichitr's allegory: Jahangir on an hourglass throne gives a book to a Sufi shaikh while an Ottoman sultan and James I of England wait below. The painter shows himself in the corner. The English king follows an English portrait of the kind Roe's embassy brought to court.
images.credit: Bichitr; Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian, F1942.15a

images.title: Emperor Jahangir Embraces Shah Abbas
images.caption: Abu'l Hasan's allegory of a meeting that never happened: a large, haloed Jahangir embraces a smaller Shah Abbas. It was painted in the years when Bishandas was in Persia taking the shah's likeness.
images.credit: Abu'l Hasan; Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian, F1945.9a

images.title: A turkey cock
images.caption: Mansur's signed portrait of an American bird that reached Jahangir through Portuguese Goa. It is an early example of the natural-history pictures the emperor ordered whenever something new came to court.
images.credit: Mansur; Victoria and Albert Museum, IM.135-1921
